title: Topic 2 - Filters & Pipes
notes: Filters and Pipes are one of Unix’s most powerful features: they allow chaining simple commands into complex workflows by passing the output of one command as the input to the next.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
The `grep` command searches for text patterns in files or input streams. It supports basic regular expressions such as `.`, `[]`, `[^]`, `*`, `^`, and `$`.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
Extended regular expressions require `egrep` or `grep -E`, adding operators like `?`, `+`, `{n,m}`, and grouping `(pat1|pat2)`.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
Common `grep` flags: `-c` (count), `-i` (ignore case), `-l` (list filenames), `-n` (line numbers), `-v` (invert match), `-w` (whole words), `-o` (only matching part).
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
The `sed` command is a stream editor that can substitute or delete lines using regex. Syntax: `sed -e 's/pattern/replacement/' file`.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
To replace globally across a line in sed, add `g` as in `sed -e 's/foo/bar/g'`. To delete matching lines, use `sed -e '/pattern/d'`.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
The `tr` command translates or deletes characters. Examples: `tr A-Z a-z` (lowercase), `tr -d '0-9'` (remove digits).
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
Flags for `tr`: `-c` complement set, `-s` squeeze repeats, `-d` delete characters. Example: `tr -cs A-Za-z '\n'` splits words onto new lines.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
The `sort` command orders lines of text. By default it sorts alphabetically. Use `-n` for numeric, `-r` for reverse, `-u` for unique.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
You can sort by columns with `-k`. Example: `sort -k2,2 file` sorts based on the 2nd field. Combine multiple keys for tie-breaking.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
The `cut` command selects portions of lines by byte (`-b`) or field (`-f`). Example: `cut -f1,3 -d',' file.csv` extracts first and third CSV columns.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
The `paste` command merges files line by line with a delimiter. Example: `paste file1 file2` produces side-by-side output.
Generated Textbook On Topics.pdf
With `paste -d` you can set custom delimiters, and combined with `sed` you can produce CSV outputs.
